identification.name: Magnesium AZ31B-H24
identification.common_form_notes: H24 (strain-hardened, partially annealed) hard-rolled sheet is the standard, most commonly cited AZ31B condition — a good strength/formability balance versus the fully-soft O temper or the more heavily strain-hardened H26.
identification.notes: The lightest common structural metal in this database (1.77 g/cm³, roughly 2/3 the density of aluminum) — deliberately chosen for weight-critical structural applications, not purely a comparison curiosity. SAFETY: magnesium fines/chips are flammable and can ignite during machining if heat builds up — use sharp tooling, adequate cutting speed, and manage chip accumulation; magnesium fires must never be extinguished with water (use a Class D extinguisher or dry sand). Machinability is rated 100% (relative rating) by this source — magnesium alloys are often used as the reference baseline for comparing other materials' machinability, reflecting excellent chip formation and low cutting forces. Compressive yield strength (180 MPa) is notably lower than tensile yield (220 MPa) — a real, well-known characteristic of magnesium's hexagonal close-packed (HCP) crystal structure, which deforms asymmetrically in tension vs. compression via twinning; this asymmetry is much less pronounced in cubic metals (steel, aluminum) and is worth remembering when analyzing compressive/buckling loads. Shear strength (160 MPa) is a directly-reported value, not derived. Shear modulus (17.0 GPa, not stored) is consistent with the stored E and ν: G = E/(2(1+ν)) = 45/2.7 ≈ 16.7 GPa, close to the source's direct value. Melting point is solidus (605°C); liquidus is 630°C. Electrical conductivity (18.7% IACS (International Annealed Copper Standard)) derived from the source's stated resistivity (9.20 µΩ·cm) via %IACS = (1.7241/9.20)×100.

typical_usage: Weight-critical structural components where aluminum still isn't light enough: aerospace brackets and housings, automotive parts (seat frames, steering wheels, transmission cases), laptop/electronics enclosures, and portable equipment frames. Excellent machinability and good damping capacity (vibration absorption) versus aluminum, at the cost of lower corrosion resistance and a real fire-safety consideration during machining that aluminum doesn't have.
